learningObjective: Explain how out-of-SSA translation lowers phi functions into copies at predecessor blocks and identify the swap/lost-copy problem.
irSnippet:
; SSA before out-of-SSA:
bb_merge:
  %a = phi i32 [%x, %P1], [%y, %P2]
  %b = phi i32 [%y, %P1], [%x, %P2]

; Naive lowering inserts at end of each predecessor:
; In %P1: a := x; b := y
; In %P2: a := y; b := x
; but if we later assign both phis to the same physical register class, sequential copies may lose values.
stem: During out-of-SSA translation, a compiler lowers phi functions into copies at predecessor block ends. Which statement about this lowering is correct, particularly regarding the swap / lost-copy issue?

options.text: Naive sequential copy insertion at predecessor ends can be incorrect when multiple phis form a cycle (e.g., swap: %a and %b exchange values). Correct lowering must schedule copies to respect the parallel-copy semantics of phi (all phis fire simultaneously), typically using a temporary register or scheduling algorithms like Sreedhar's or Boissinot's.
Out-of-SSA lowering trivially inserts one move per phi at the merge block; no predecessor-side changes are needed.
Out-of-SSA lowering requires all phi functions to be first converted to `select` instructions; only then can the code generator produce copies.
Modern optimizers avoid out-of-SSA lowering entirely by preserving phi nodes into machine code emission.

explanation: Phi functions have parallel-copy semantics — all phis at a block are conceptually assigned simultaneously. Naively serializing them into predecessor-block copies can miscompile swap-like patterns. Correct out-of-SSA algorithms (Sreedhar, Boissinot) either schedule copies with temporaries or use permutation-decomposition to preserve semantics. Options B, C, D contain factual errors: B ignores that phis fire from predecessor edges; C describes an unrelated substitution; D is wrong because machine code cannot express phi natively.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: parallel-copy semantics plus swap problem require careful scheduling.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: phi lowering happens at predecessor edges, not at the merge block, because each incoming value corresponds to a specific predecessor.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: converting phi to select requires speculating both branches; not applicable to control-flow merges with side effects.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: machine code has no phi instruction; SSA must be lowered before or during instruction selection.

assumptions: Standard SSA and out-of-SSA algorithms (Sreedhar, Boissinot).
Target machine code lacks a native phi instruction.
nonImplications: Does not imply out-of-SSA is the only way; SSA-based register allocation can operate directly on SSA form.
Does not imply the swap problem always occurs; simple non-cyclic phi patterns lower without temporaries.

distractorRationales.D: Falsely claims machine code supports phi.
